GLiNER2.5: Candle Metal and Swift/MLXTechnical report — macOS Apple Silicon and iOS

This report compares two Apple GPU paths for the Boundary/DeBERTa-v2 models in apiplant/gliner-rs: the existing Rust implementation using Candle Metal, and the Swift implementation using MLX Metal. Correctness, request latency, model loading and process memory are evaluated separately. The earlier CPU/GPU benchmark remains as historical evidence and does not determine the backend choice.

Implementation baseline: 450367e. Review and documentation updates: PR #1.

Candle comparison implementation: source revision. Executable and numerical-source hashes are embedded with each benchmark.

Candle Metal versus MLX Metal

Recorded GPU comparison evidence is loaded from the embedded data.

Correctness gate

The full 28-case suite covers entities, classification, relations, records and attributes. Exact discrete values and array order are checked; floating confidence values use the existing absolute tolerance of 1e-4. Full final encoder outputs use 1e-3. Agreement with the CPU reference and direct agreement between GPU engines are reported separately; a bounded near-tie exception against CPU is never presented as strict parity.

Target / checkpointCompared outputsStrict casesMax confidence deltaNotes

Latency on the same GPU

The engines use F32 with MLX TF32 disabled. The selected dataset provides the trial and timing method below. Latency is the median of process medians; pooled p95 is descriptive. Validation results and individual samples are recorded in the embedded data.

RequestBackendLatency median / p95 (ms)Load median (ms)Peak physical footprint range (MiB)Peak process RSS range (MiB)

Apple describes memory footprint as the charged dirty/compressed memory of CPU and GPU resources on Apple Silicon; clean read-only file mappings may be resident without contributing to that footprint. See Apple’s memory profiling explanation. Physical footprint and RSS answer different questions.

Mac CLI timings include JSON serialization and synchronous stdout writing. iPhone timings include the Rust JSON bridge and output conversion, but exclude writing diagnostic JSONL records and actor/UI scheduling. Absolute times must not be compared across these two harnesses. Mac MLX uses automatic cache retention; iPhone MLX uses the platform policy of 20 MiB with clearing after each request. Candle retains its existing allocator and cache policy; the changes below reduce temporary tensors and weight-loading residency.

Load timings can be affected by filesystem and shader caches; these measurements are not a controlled cold-start experiment. Backend order rotates within each of three trials. Mac uses 54 fresh processes; iPhone uses 18 fresh processes with three requests each. Each device records 1,890 calls including 270 warm-ups; all outputs were checked. No steady-idle residency measurement was made.

Physical memory on the mixed long suite

The short requests above do not exercise the largest attention tensors. A separate diagnostic executes the mixed core suite on Mac (21 cases) and the full suite on iPhone (28 cases), including the long-input case. Each configuration ran once; these are process peaks, not repeated latency benchmarks. Mac MLX was not remeasured for this diagnostic.

Device / checkpointCases / runsOriginal Candle physical peak (MiB)Optimized Candle physical peak (MiB)MLX physical peak (MiB)Candle reduction

The fused attention epilogue reduces transient allocations at long sequence lengths: measured physical peaks fall 21–28% across these diagnostics. For the short Mac requests, the streaming/pipeline overhead instead raises the physical peak by 0.3–2.7%; iPhone Multi is approximately unchanged. Post-load model footprint is also approximately unchanged. These results do not establish a universal memory reduction. Mac RSS falls 68–84%, largely due to loading/accounting changes; it is not an equivalent reduction in charged physical memory.

Mac peaks use /usr/bin/time -l; iPhone peaks use task_vm_info.ledger_phys_footprint_peak, sampled outside request timers. RSS and physical footprint overlap and must not be added. iPhone Multi MLX has a 176.845 ms pooled p95 on apple_ceo; its tail samples remain in the tables and raw data.

Rust optimization and controls

ChangeMechanismBoundary / opt-out
Weight loadingValidate safetensors header, then stream exact-size weights without mapping the full file. macOS: Private buffers with at most 16 MiB Shared staging. iOS: read directly into Shared buffers.--metal-mmap restores the original loader. Loading can be slower; weight-buffer sizes were already exact in the original path.
Attention score epilogueOne custom F32 Metal dispatch combines relative gathers, content/relative sums, scaling and masking. Avoids head-expanded index copies, two full gathered tensors and a dense floor tensor. Pipeline cached per encoder.--metal-original-attention restores the original path. Other dtypes retain it. QK scores and softmax remain dense O(B·heads·T²); this is not FlashAttention.
Relative indicesCompute the 2T−1 unique log-bucket distances once, then fill T² indices.No persistent shape cache; no change to bucket values.
Arithmetic verificationFast math disabled, explicit FMA for scaling, original finite F32 mask floor. Tests include batches, padding, transposed/noncontiguous inputs, nonzero offsets and cancellation-sensitive values.56 complete outputs and 3,109,248 final encoder states match original Candle bit-for-bit on Mac. This does not imply bitwise identity across CPU and GPU engines.

Both optimizations default on for Rust Metal. The two CLI flags are independent; passing both restores the original configuration. RustLoadOptions exposes the same choices. The C API uses bit 0 for mmap and bit 1 for original attention (0 = optimized; 3 = original). The demo’s “Rust optimizations” switch selects these combined modes and reloads the model. CPU/CUDA and Swift/MLX arithmetic remain unchanged; no Candle fork is required.

Implementation cost and remaining limits

The Rust model is reused. Implementation changes and their measured effects are described in the selected dataset and embedded provenance. Metal is opt-in and initialization failure is an error, with no CPU fallback. The iPhone integration uses a Rust static library and a small C boundary called from SwiftUI. A Swift rewrite is not required to use Metal or build an iPhone app.

These workloads establish numerical agreement and local performance for the tested checkpoints. They do not measure dataset-level extraction quality, energy, sustained thermal behavior, every Apple device, or minimum supported OS versions. Similar output does not by itself establish similar performance or memory use.

01Scope and repository structure

Both backends live in the existing repository. Rust/Candle now supports opt-in Metal in addition to its existing CPU/CUDA paths. The Swift implementation uses MLX tensor operations. Both paths use Metal kernels for GPU execution. The following implementation and runtime sections primarily document the Swift/MLX path.

PathResponsibility
swift/Sources/GLiNERMLX/Tokenizer, schema preparation, DeBERTa encoder, Boundary heads, decoding, batching, chunking, runtime configuration
swift/Sources/GLiNERCLI/Local model loading, extraction requests, diagnostics and per-request timing
ios/GLiNERDemo/Shared SwiftUI application for iOS and macOS; serialized model worker and offline checkpoint reuse
src/, examples/apple_reference.rsExisting Rust model, opt-in Metal CLI, CPU/Metal output and encoder exporters
ffi/Rust static library and documented C ownership/error boundary for the Apple demo
scripts/Pinned checkpoint download, numerical comparison, Mac/device verification and benchmarks

Supported tasks: entity extraction, single/multi-label classification, relations, structured records in natural/latent/anchorless modes, choice fields, entity attributes, regex validators, overlap policies, padded batches, and long-document chunking. Legacy Span checkpoints, ModernBERT encoders and quantized weights are outside the implemented scope.

Declared deployment targets: macOS 14 and iOS 17. Actual execution was verified on macOS 27.2 and a physical iPhone 17 Pro; minimum OS versions were not tested on devices running those versions.

StageImplementationExecution

DeBERTa attention

For input IDs and mask shaped [B,T], hidden states have shape [B,T,H]. Attention projections are reshaped to [B,A,T,H/A]. The implementation combines content-to-content, content-to-position and position-to-content scores, using the same relative-position bucketing and masking semantics as the reference.

S = (Q Kᵀ + gather(Q Rkᵀ, c2p) + transpose(gather(K Rqᵀ, p2c))) / √(3 · head_dim)
context = softmax(mask(S)) V
attended = LayerNorm(Wo(context) + hidden)
next_hidden = LayerNorm(W2(GELU_erf(W1(attended))) + attended)

Relative embeddings are normalized and their layer-specific projected keys/queries are computed once during model initialization. The pinned checkpoints use shared attention keys, 256 position buckets and LayerNorm ε = 1e-7. Dropout is omitted in inference.

Memory complexity: this encoder explicitly constructs dense attention scores and relative-position index matrices. Attention storage scales as O(B · A · T²). A local mask in the Boundary head does not make the DeBERTa encoder sparse. Swift/MLX uses separate tensor operations here. Rust/Candle now fuses the score epilogue described above; neither path removes the dense attention matrix.

Boundary and record configuration

The tested checkpoints use boundary dimension 128, two boundary attention layers with four heads and window 128, one refinement layer, shared pool size 192 and boundary top-k 32. Relation pairs are capped at 64; the record head has 32 learned instance queries. Candidate selection and exclusivity constraints preserve reference tie-breaking. Scalar exclusive record fields use a linear assignment solver.

Source: Deberta.swift, BoundaryHead.swift, RecordHead.swift, Model.swift.

03Checkpoint inventory

All three tested checkpoints contain 334 tensors stored as F32 in model.safetensors. The loader casts encoder tensors to the selected runtime precision and retains the extraction heads in F32. Parameter counts below are calculated from the safetensors headers, including the task heads.

VariantParametersLayersHiddenHeadsFFNVocabularyWeights, MB

MB and GB use decimal bytes; MiB uses 2²⁰ bytes. Weight size excludes tokenizer/configuration files. Total download sizes and revision/checksum values are in the provenance table. The new GPU comparison tests Small and Multi; the historical CPU/GPU and profile experiments use Multi.

Pinned revisions, download sizes and SHA-256
CheckpointDownload bytesRevision / weights SHA-256

The default input guard is 4,096 tokens including the schema. Oversized requests fail explicitly rather than silently truncating. extractLong splits text into overlapping word chunks and remaps/deduplicates predictions. max_position_embeddings = 512 in the encoder configuration is not used as a silent 512-token truncation rule.

04Precision and memory controls

ProfileEncoder / headsmacOS cacheiOS cacheClear after requestTF32
accurateF32 / F32Original MLX policy20 MiBmacOS: no; iOS: yesOff
fastF16 / F32Original MLX policy20 MiBNoOff
low-memoryF16 / F3220 MiB20 MiBYesOff

CLI overrides are independent: --fp16/--fp32, --tf32/--no-tf32, --cache-mb auto|N and --clear-cache/--retain-cache. A cache value of zero disables unused-buffer retention. These limits concern reusable buffers, not the total weights or total process memory.

Configuration lifetime

  • Precision changes reload the model and convert encoder weights once.
  • Cache limit and clearing policy can change between requests without reloading weights.
  • MLX runtime settings are process-wide. Model calls should be serialized, including calls across models with different cache policies.
  • Request-scoped autorelease pools release Foundation temporaries before optional MLX cache clearing.

TF32 constraints

  • MLX 0.33 caches its TF32 choice at the first relevant computation.
  • Set MLX_ENABLE_TF32 through the runtime API before any MLX workload in a host app.
  • The SDK rejects a late change after its model has started computation; the demo requires a process restart.
  • M3 has no applicable MLX NAX/TF32 path. No TF32 speedup was measured on this Mac.

F16 is approximate. In an exploratory 21-case comparison using a confidence tolerance of 0.02, small matched 20/21 cases and multi 18/21. That tolerance is looser than the F32 acceptance criterion. Deviations include a relation boundary, confidence differences exceeding 0.02 and different selected candidates. F32 with TF32 disabled is the reference-parity configuration.

Source: Runtime.swift. The demo labels are Italian: “Precisione”, “Velocità” and “Memoria ridotta”.

5.3 Precision/cache experiment

A separate session measured five GPU configurations × three texts × 35 calls = 525 executions. The paired comparison above added three fresh GPU processes and six CPU processes, totaling 315 executions. Values from the two sessions are not interchangeable baselines.

Median request time; F16 bars indicate approximate arithmetic.

EncoderCache / clear64 words median / p9597 words median / p95130 words median / p95

F32 outputs were bit-identical across the three cache configurations. Automatic cache had the lowest F32 median on these workloads. F16/automatic cache reduced median latency by approximately 9–10%, but exceeded the strict reference tolerance; it is an opt-in trade-off. These runs do not establish a peak-memory reduction for any profile.

F16 confidence differences from the same-session F32 baseline reached 0.000287235, 0.000316262 and 0.004377604 for the three texts. The longest text also reversed the order of the Torino and Bologna entities. The later paired-comparison session's F32 medians were approximately 12–14% higher than the earlier profile session. This between-session variation exceeds the observed F16 reduction; the F16 result is an observation from that session, not a statistically established general speedup.

5.4 First request and UI smoke test

In the profile session, the first recorded F32 process took 1,678.919 ms to load and 1,693.249 ms for its first request. Subsequent process loads and first-call timings benefited from system caches. These values do not support a general cold-start comparison with Rust.

A separate Release macOS demo smoke test used the short “Michele vive a Milano e lavora per Acme.” input, three labels and multi/F32/automatic cache. First call including loading: 1,251.326 ms. Four subsequent calls: 57.608, 47.763, 54.531 and 41.933 ms; JSON formatting: 0.046–0.057 ms. This is a manual UI sample, not a paired benchmark or a p95 estimate. Its timer covers the model worker and excludes rendering/actor queue delay.

Ordering exception

In the long-input case (zero-based case 7), two “Berlin” entity spans at code-point offsets [2701,2707) and [457,463) swap order. The Rust confidence range is 1.1920928955078125e-7; the MLX scores are tied. The comparator only accepts contiguous blocks of identical entity identities whose confidence range is at most 1e-6 on both sides. It records every accepted reorder. Record, relation and classification arrays remain strictly ordered.

07Historical MLX trace and iOS integration

The app was built for a physical iPhone, signed using existing local development signing material and installed for testing. Models were copied to the app’s Documents storage for offline self-tests. The verifier uses a unique run ID and rejects stale result files.

28-case F32 runLoad, sInference sum, sPeak RSS, bytesMLX active peak, bytes
small0.5392812.052728592,855,040Not recorded
multi1.3313982.7156621,492,697,0882,673,877,508

The case set mixes task types and input lengths; the sums are extraction timers, not whole-run durations or throughput benchmarks. Both verified runs also exported full final encoder outputs. JSON serialization/writing, the additional encoder pass and trace export are excluded from the extraction-time sums but contribute to the diagnostic workload and memory observations. Process RSS and MLX allocation accounting overlap and must not be added. Neither is a guaranteed memory ceiling. No profile-by-profile RSS/energy/thermal comparison was performed.

Integration contract

  • Load local config.json, encoder_config/config.json, tokenizer.json and model.safetensors.
  • Use one serialized worker for a model. The demo uses a Swift actor; the numerical API itself is synchronous.
  • Keep the model resident between requests. Changing only the cache policy does not require weight reload.
  • Configure TF32 before any other MLX computation in the host process. The runtime cannot detect an earlier computation performed by unrelated libraries.
  • Do not interpret the 20 MiB cache limit as a 20 MiB model-memory budget.
import Foundation
import GLiNERMLX

actor Extractor {
    private let model: GLiNERModel

    init(directory: URL) throws {
        model = try GLiNERModel(
            modelDirectory: directory,
            precision: .float32,
            runtimeConfiguration: .platformDefault)
    }

    func extract(_ text: String) throws -> JSONValue {
        try model.extract(
            text,
            schema: Schema(entities: ["person", "company", "location"]),
            options: .init(includeSpans: true, includeConfidence: true))
    }
}

Additional API: extractBatch, extractLong, classifyText, classificationProbabilities, extractRelations, extractJSON, prepare, encode and updateRuntimeConfiguration.

09Limitations and remaining engineering work

AreaCurrent boundaryRequired evidence for expansion
ArchitecturesBoundary + DeBERTa-v2 only; tested small/base/multi checkpointsAdditional architecture implementation and independent parity suites for other model families
Numerical identityF32 tolerance-based agreement; multi has one near-tie reorder. F16 is not parity-equivalent.Model/task-specific regression evaluation before changing the default arithmetic
GPU optimizationCustom Candle F32 score epilogue; existing MLX kernels; dense QK/softmax and CPU candidate/record decoding remainProfile dense attention, graph compilation and synchronization before further changes; rerun full parity checks
Memory / quantizationF32 checkpoints; optional F16 encoder; cache controls; no quantized load pathQuantization calibration and accuracy evaluation; matched peak-memory/energy measurements
Performance coverageOne Mac and one physical iPhone; Small/Multi F32; three batch-1 NER texts; multiple process trialsLong-input scaling, batching, other tasks, other Apple chips, thermal/energy instrumentation and sustained workloads
Device coveragePhysical iPhone 17 Pro and Mac M3 Pro; minimum declared OS versions not exercisedOlder-device memory/compatibility testing and minimum-OS execution
Product distributionLocal development build and demo projectApplication integration, lifecycle/memory-pressure handling, packaging and distribution validation

The evidence covers two working GPU implementations for the stated checkpoints and devices. Bitwise identity was established for the optimized versus original Candle runs on Mac; cross-engine agreement uses declared tolerances. Device compatibility, distribution readiness and performance outside the measured workloads remain unverified.
